questions.question: A class is told to use `set.seed(2026)` for a simulation, but one student writes `set.seed(7)` at the top of her script instead. Which statement about her draws is correct?
options: They equal her classmates' draws, only shifted by 2019 places in the stream.
They differ from her classmates' draws but are just as random and reproducible.
They are smaller on average, since a small seed gives small random numbers.
They equal her classmates' draws, since any seed fixes the same stream.

questions.question: A student on Windows and a grader on a Mac both run `set.seed(77); rnorm(2)` in R 4.3 with the default generator settings, and both see the same two numbers. Why is this possible?
options: R looks up the two draws for seed 77 in a stored table of random numbers.
`rnorm()` gives these same two numbers on every computer, even without a seed.
Both computers read the system clock, and the seed sets both clocks alike.
The draws come from a deterministic algorithm whose starting state the seed fixes.

questions.question: A student's simulation script starts with `set.seed(2026)` and then makes several random calls. A grader runs the script on another computer. What else must hold for the grader to get exactly the student's draws?
options: The same random calls run in the same order, with the same generator settings.
The script runs on the same type of computer and the same operating system.
The same random calls run after the seed, in whatever order the grader likes.
The grader runs it in a fresh R session, since an open session ignores the seed.

questions.question: After a single `set.seed(5)`, the call `sample(1:10, 3)` is run twice in a row and the two results differ. Why do they differ, although the seed is fixed?
options: `set.seed()` fixes only the first random call; the second call is unseeded.
The second call avoids the three values drawn by the first call.
The second call takes the next numbers of the stream, after the first call's.
R increases the seed by one after every call, so the second call uses seed 6.

questions.question: The line `x <- sample(1:6, 2); set.seed(1); y <- rnorm(2)` is run, and later run again in a new R session. Which objects are certain to get the same values in both runs?
options: Both `x` and `y`
Only `x`
Neither `x` nor `y`
Only `y`

questions.question: Which of these four lines makes `identical(a, b)` return `TRUE`?
options: `set.seed(42); a <- runif(3); b <- runif(3)`
`set.seed(42); a <- runif(3); rnorm(5); set.seed(42); b <- runif(3)`
`set.seed(42); a <- runif(3); set.seed(43); b <- runif(3)`
`set.seed(42); a <- runif(3); set.seed(42); rnorm(1); b <- runif(3)`

questions.question: After `x <- numeric(5); for (i in 1:5) { set.seed(3); x[i] <- sample(1:10, 1) }`, what does `x` contain?
options: Five numbers that vary within `x` and are the same on every run
Five numbers that vary within `x` and change on every run
One number repeated five times, the same on every run
The number `3` five times, the value given to `set.seed()`

questions.question: Script A is `set.seed(4); a <- sample(1:50, 2); m <- mean(c(2, 8)); b <- sample(1:50, 2)`. Script B is the same without the statement `m <- mean(c(2, 8))`. How do the two vectors `b` compare?
options: They are identical: `mean()` draws no random numbers.
They differ: every statement after `set.seed()` moves the stream on.
They differ: a seed only covers the statement directly after it.
They are identical: after one seed, `b` is always a copy of `a`.

questions.question: Which line simulates 1000 rolls of a fair die so that the rolls vary and the whole vector `rolls` is the same every time the line is run?
options: `rolls <- replicate(1000, sample(1:6, 1)); set.seed(1)`
`set.seed(1); rolls <- rep(sample(1:6, 1), 1000)`
`rolls <- replicate(1000, sample(1:6, 1))`
`set.seed(1); rolls <- replicate(1000, sample(1:6, 1))`

questions.question: A script reads `set.seed(7); a <- sample(1:20, 3); b <- runif(2); d <- sample(1:20, 3)`. A colleague deletes the statement `b <- runif(2)` and reruns it. Which results keep their values?
options: Both `a` and `d`: `runif()` and `sample()` use separate streams.
Only `a`: `d` now starts where `b` used to start.
Neither: any edit to a seeded script changes all of its draws.
Both `a` and `d`: the seed fixes each `sample()` call by itself.

questions.question: A report written with R 3.5 shows the output of `set.seed(10); sample(1:20, 4)`. In R 4.3 the same line gives four different numbers. What explains the difference?
options: A seed reproduces draws only on the computer where they were first made.
R 4.x ignores `set.seed()` unless `RNGkind()` is called earlier in the script.
Since R 3.6.0, `sample()` uses `"Rejection"` sampling instead of `"Rounding"`.
Every new R version changes all generators, so no seeded result carries over.

questions.question: A student runs `set.seed(5); p_hat <- mean(rbinom(200, 1, 0.3))` five times and gets `0.325` every time. She concludes that her estimate of the probability 0.3 has no simulation error. Which statement is correct?
options: Each run repeats the same 200 draws, so the error is that of one run of 200 draws.
She is right: identical reruns show the estimate has settled on the true value.
The five equal runs together give the precision of 1000 independent draws.
The error can only be judged without a seed, since seeded draws are not random.

questions.question: To compare the average daily cost of ordering 20 units with that of ordering 24 units, a student runs `set.seed(1); d <- rpois(1000, 20)` before computing the cost for 20, and the same line again before computing the cost for 24. What does repeating the seed achieve?
options: The second demand vector is independent of the first, which makes the comparison fair.
It is a mistake, as both costs now rest on the same demand and say nothing.
It makes both average costs equal to the true expected costs of the two orders.
Both order sizes are judged on the same 1000 simulated days of demand.

questions.question: Do `set.seed(2); a <- runif(1) + rnorm(1)` and `set.seed(2); b <- rnorm(1) + runif(1)` give the same value, and why?
options: Yes: addition is commutative, so swapping the two terms changes nothing.
No: the two calls run in the other order and take other numbers from the stream.
Yes: `runif()` and `rnorm()` each take their numbers from their own stream.
No: the seed only covers the first call, so the second term is unseeded.

questions.question: An old analysis made with R 3.5 printed the output of `set.seed(31); sample(1:8, 3)`. Which line makes R 4.3 reproduce exactly those three draws?
options: `set.seed(31, sample.kind = "Rounding"); sample(1:8, 3)`
`set.seed(31, sample.kind = "Rejection"); sample(1:8, 3)`
`set.seed(31); RNGkind(); sample(1:8, 3)`
`set.seed(31, normal.kind = "Rounding"); sample(1:8, 3)`

questions.question: Which of these four lines gives the same `z` as `set.seed(5); z <- rnorm(1)`?
options: `set.seed(5); x <- 1; if (x > 0) u <- runif(1); z <- rnorm(1)`
`set.seed(5); x <- runif(1); if (x > 2) u <- 0; z <- rnorm(1)`
`set.seed(5); x <- -1; if (x > 0) u <- runif(1); z <- rnorm(1)`
`set.seed(5); u <- runif(1); set.seed(6); z <- rnorm(1)`

questions.question: A student estimates a probability whose true value is 0.25 by simulating 500 draws. She tries seeds 1 to 50 and reports the run with seed 37, whose estimate is closest to 0.25. What is wrong with reporting it?
options: Nothing, as she reports seed 37 too, so a grader can rerun the very same draws.
Seed 37 also gives the most accurate estimate with 5000 draws, so she should use that.
Nothing: seed 37 suits this problem best, so its runs should be used from now on.
Seed 37 is not more accurate; the best of 50 runs hides the error of a typical run.

questions.question: A student runs `res <- numeric(100); for (i in 1:100) { set.seed(i); res[i] <- mean(sample(1:6, 10, replace = TRUE)) }`. Which statement about `res` is correct?
options: All 100 values in `res` are equal, as always happens with a seed inside a loop.
Rerunning the loop reproduces `res`, and the 100 experiments use different streams.
`res` changes on every rerun, since the seed keeps changing inside the loop.
Experiment `i + 1` repeats experiment `i` shifted by one draw, as seed `i + 1` continues seed `i`.

questions.question: After `set.seed(9); a <- rnorm(5); set.seed(9); b <- c(rnorm(3), rnorm(2))`, how does `b` relate to `a`?
options: No element of `b` equals the matching element of `a`
`b` is identical to `a`
`b[1:3]` equals `a[1:3]`, but `b[4:5]` differs from `a[4:5]`

questions.question: After `f <- function() { set.seed(1); sample(1:6, 1) }; set.seed(99); f(); u <- runif(1)`, which line gives the same value as `u`?
options: `set.seed(1); sample(1:6, 1); runif(1)`
`set.seed(99); runif(1)`
`set.seed(99); sample(1:6, 1); runif(1)`
`set.seed(1); runif(1)`
